messages.summary:
## Objective
- Extend the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR into a complete, playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note them on completion.

## Decisions
- Continue the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected existing game files and confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present at that point.

### Active
- Map gameplay hooks and UI IDs, then implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining portions of existing files for interaction hooks and UI IDs.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

## Objective
- Extend the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR into a complete, playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note them on completion.

## Decisions
- Continue the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the existing game files and confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present at that point.

### Active
- Map gameplay hooks and UI IDs, then implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining portions of existing files for interaction hooks and UI IDs.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

## Findings for `main.js`

All details below are from **`/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/js/lore.js`**. There is no `main.js` or separate case-data module in the project’s `js/` directory.

### Locations and map data

- **`LOCATIONS`** (lines 18–39) is an object keyed by location ID, such as `precinct`, `chapel`, `hospital`, `foundry`, and `chapelBasement`. Each entry supplies `name`, `short`, world coordinates (`x`, `z`), dimensions (`w`, `d`, `h`), `kind`, `color`, and `spot`; many also define `door` and `interior`. The basement additionally has `under: true`.
- **`SCENE_ANCHORS`** (41–47) lists five notable scene positions, each with `id`, associated `loc`, 3D `pos`, `angle`, and `label`.
- **`KEY_PLACES`** (49–62) is a shorter, UI-oriented list of 12 locations with `id`, `label`, and `icon`.
- **`TOWN`** (6–12) provides Mercy Falls’ name, county, population, founding year, and tagline.

### NPC cast shape

- **`CAST`** (96–347) is an array of 16 character objects, keyed by `id`. Common fields include identity and role (`name`, `short`, `age`, `sex`, `role`, `job`), location IDs (`workplace`, `home`), appearance (`color`, `accent`, `skin`, `hair`, `build`), and forensic `traits`.
- Most NPCs also have `alibi`, `alibiWitness`, `alibiTruth`, `alibiWeak`, `sect`, `public`, `suspect`, `secret`, `motive`, and dialogue fields (`greeting`, `victimTalk`, `sectTalk`, `pressure`, `asylum`). Some have additional `witness`, `witnessLine`, or `missing` flags.
- **`SUSPECT_IDS`** (349) identifies the five suspects: `silas`, `edith`, `jonah`, `caleb`, `isaac`.
- **`WITNESS_LINES`** (350–357) maps witness IDs to testimony strings.

### Evidence and forensic clues

There is **no exported evidence list or evidence-object schema** in `lore.js`. The closest foundation for implementing evidence is the `CAST[].traits` object: it contains `hand`, `shoe`, `fiber`, `ash`, and `handwrite`; the comment at lines 94–95 says these are identifying traits for a forensic loop, and that only the Hand’s set appears in physical evidence. `WITNESS_LINES`, alibis, and character dialogue also provide investigative clues, but evidence items and collection logic would need to be defined elsewhere or added by `main.js`.

### Endings

**`ENDINGS`** (404–455) is an object keyed by ending ID. Each entry has `title`, `eyebrow`, and `text`. The keys are `best`, `capture`, `wrong`, `escape`, `sect`, `conspiracy`, `supernatural`, `compromised`, `cold`, and `death`.

### Cases and variable case data

- There is **no `CASES` export** and no explicit case progression structure in `lore.js`. The case number `09-114` appears in ending eyebrow strings; it is not part of a case object.
- The variable victim-related data is **`VICTIM_TEMPLATES`** (67–89): a static array of three victim objects—Maren Holt (`maren`), Elias Ward (`deacon`), and Cora Lin (`songbird`). Each has `id`, `name`, `age`, `job`, `home`, `link`, `epithet`, `hair`, `eyes`, `detail`, and `nextOfKin`.
- This array is the only evident template-style case variation in the file. It does not define case IDs, sequencing, evidence, suspects per case, or endings per case; those relationships would need to be implemented separately.

## Objective
- Extend the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR into a complete, playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note them on completion.

## Decisions
- Continue the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the game interface, world/interior APIs, and narrative data; confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present at that point.

### Active
- Map gameplay hooks and UI IDs, then implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining portions of existing files for interaction hooks and UI IDs.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

## Objective
- Extend the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR into a complete, playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note them on completion.

## Decisions
- Continue the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

How to Investigate

123:
124:

Move

W A S D walk, Shift run, mouse to look. Click the scene to capture the cursor. Esc releases it.

125:

Work the scene

Approach the glinting markers and press E. Every piece of evidence is logged to your casebook. Some clues only resolve in the lab.

126:

Casebook

Tab opens the case file: evidence, suspects, map, the sect, notes. You can fast-travel to known locations from the map.

127:

Interviews

Press E on a person. Ask about the victim, the sect, alibis. Present evidence to break a story. People remember how you treat them.

128:

Warrant

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

129:

Stay human

Sleep, eat, and keep your stress down. The town does not pause for you, and the killer is watching how you work.

## Objective
- Extend the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR into a complete, playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note them on completion.

## Decisions
- Continue the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

Move

Work the scene

Approach the glinting markers and press E. Every piece of evidence is logged to your casebook. Some clues only resolve in the lab.

Casebook

Tab opens the case file: evidence, suspects, map, the sect, notes. You can fast-travel to known locations from the map.

Interviews

Press E on a person. Ask about the victim, the sect, alibis. Present evidence to break a story. People remember how you treat them.

Warrant

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

Sleep, eat, and keep your stress down. The town does not pause for you, and the killer is watching how you work.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note them on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

How to Investigate

124:

Move

W A S D walk, Shift run, mouse to look. Click the scene to capture the cursor. Esc releases it.

125:

Work the scene

Approach the glinting markers and press E. Every piece of evidence is logged to your casebook. Some clues only resolve in the lab.

126:

Casebook

Tab opens the case file: evidence, suspects, map, the sect, notes. You can fast-travel to known locations from the map.

127:

Interviews

Press E on a person. Ask about the victim, the sect, alibis. Present evidence to break a story. People remember how you treat them.

128:

Warrant

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

129:

Stay human

Sleep, eat, and keep your stress down. The town does not pause for you, and the killer is watching how you work.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, audio utilities, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, audio utilities, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

Move

W A S D walk, Shift run, mouse to look. Click the scene to capture the cursor. Esc releases it.

Work the scene

Approach the glinting markers and press E. Every piece of evidence is logged to your casebook. Some clues only resolve in the lab.

Casebook

Tab opens the case file: evidence, suspects, map, the sect, notes. You can fast-travel to known locations from the map.

Interviews

Press E on a person. Ask about the victim, the sect, alibis. Present evidence to break a story. People remember how you treat them.

Warrant

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, audio utilities, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places and organizations are fictional.

1: ## Process lifecycle
2: 
3: - Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
4: - Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
5: - After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.

7: ## Linux browser and WebGPU capture
8: 
9: - Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
12: - Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
13: - Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
14: - Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
15: - Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
16: - Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
17: - Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, audio utilities, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places and organizations are fictional.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected the interface, world/interior APIs, narrative data, audio utilities, and project files.
- Confirmed `index.html` references a missing `js/main.js` entry point.
- Checked repository status; no changes were present.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining interface IDs and world/interior interaction hooks as needed.
2. Implement `js/main.js` with the core playable systems.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game interface and reference to the missing entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town construction and world API.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments and evidence objects.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.

Move

W A S D walk, Shift run, mouse to look. Click the scene to capture the cursor. Esc releases it.

Work the scene

Approach the glinting markers and press E. Every piece of evidence is logged to your casebook. Some clues only resolve in the lab.

Casebook

Tab opens the case file: evidence, suspects, map, the sect, notes. You can fast-travel to known locations from the map.

Interviews

Press E on a person. Ask about the victim, the sect, alibis. Present evidence to break a story. People remember how you treat them.

128:

Warrant

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

Stay human

Sleep, eat, and keep your stress down. The town does not pause for you, and the killer is watching how you work.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.
- Implement the missing `js/main.js` entry point to connect the existing world, interiors, interface, and narrative systems.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

- Identified existing portal and evidence interaction records in `js/interiors.js`.

- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

- (none)

- `index.html`: Game UI and module entry point.

- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments, evidence objects, and portals.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.
- Portal interactables expose `kind: 'portal'`, `destinationPosition`, and `from`/`to`; evidence interactables expose `kind: 'evidence'`, `description`, and `location`.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.
- Implement the missing `js/main.js` entry point to connect the existing world, interiors, interface, and narrative systems.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected `index.html`, `js/world.js`, `js/interiors.js`, `js/lore.js`, `js/util.js`, `js/audio.js`, and `README.md`.
- Confirmed `index.html` loads the missing `js/main.js`.
- Identified portal interactables (`kind: 'portal'`, `destinationPosition`, `from`/`to`) and evidence interactables (`kind: 'evidence'`, `description`, `location`) in `js/interiors.js`.
- No files have been edited or committed.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining world APIs, NPC data, and interface behavior needed for integration.
2. Implement `js/main.js` using the existing world and narrative structures.
3. Run available checks and verify the game in a browser; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game UI and module entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town, player-world support, and world data.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments, evidence objects, and portals.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.
- `world.js` has scene/world construction and collections including `colliders`, `interactables`, `interactablesById`, `interiors`, `scenes`, `keyNpcs`, `genericNpc`, and `genericList`.
- Portal interactables are defined in `js/interiors.js` by `addPortalPair`; use their destination positions to travel between street and interiors.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.
- Implement the missing `js/main.js` entry point to connect the existing world, interiors, interface, and narrative systems.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected `index.html`, `js/world.js`, `js/interiors.js`, `js/lore.js`, `js/util.js`, `js/audio.js`, and `README.md`.
- Confirmed `index.html` loads the missing `js/main.js`; identified portal and evidence interactable conventions in `js/interiors.js`.

### Active
- Inspect remaining world APIs, NPC data, and interface behavior, then implement `js/main.js`.
- Run available checks and verify the game in a browser.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect world, NPC, and interface APIs needed for integration.
2. Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.
3. Run checks and browser verification; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game UI and module entry point.
- `js/main.js`: Missing entry point to implement.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town, player-world support, and world data.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments, evidence objects, and portals.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.
- `world.js` provides collections including `colliders`, `interactables`, `interactablesById`, `interiors`, `scenes`, `keyNpcs`, `genericNpc`, and `genericList`.
- Portal interactables use `kind: 'portal'`, `destinationPosition`, and `from`/`to`; evidence interactables use `kind: 'evidence'`, `description`, and `location`.
- No files have been edited or committed.

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.
- Implement the missing `js/main.js` entry point to connect the existing world, interiors, interface, and narrative systems.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected `index.html`, `js/world.js`, `js/interiors.js`, `js/lore.js`, `js/util.js`, `js/audio.js`, and `README.md`.
- Confirmed `index.html` loads missing `js/main.js`; identified portal and evidence conventions in `js/interiors.js`.

### Active
- Inspect remaining world APIs, NPC data, and interface behavior, then implement `js/main.js`.
- Run available checks and verify the game in a browser.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect world, NPC, and interface APIs needed for integration.
2. Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, and case progression.
3. Run checks and browser verification; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game UI and module entry point.
- `js/main.js`: Missing entry point to implement.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town, player-world support, and world data.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments, evidence objects, and portals.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmospheric effects.
- `css/style.css`: Game presentation and styling.

## Important Context
- All persons, places, and organizations are fictional.
- `world.js` provides collections including `colliders`, `interactables`, `interactablesById`, `interiors`, `scenes`, `keyNpcs`, `genericNpc`, and `genericList`.
- Portal interactables use `kind: 'portal'`, `destinationPosition`, and `from`/`to`; evidence interactables use `kind: 'evidence'`, `description`, and `location`.

How to Investigate

123:
124:

Move

W A S D walk, Shift run, mouse to look. Click the scene to capture the cursor. Esc releases it.

125:

Work the scene

Approach the glinting markers and press E. Every piece of evidence is logged to your casebook. Some clues only resolve in the lab.

126:

Casebook

Tab opens the case file: evidence, suspects, map, the sect, notes. You can fast-travel to known locations from the map.

127:

Interviews

Press E on a person. Ask about the victim, the sect, alibis. Present evidence to break a story. People remember how you treat them.

128:

Warrant

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

129:

Stay human

Sleep, eat, and keep your stress down. The town does not pause for you, and the killer is watching how you work.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.
- Implement the missing `js/main.js` entry point to connect the existing world, interiors, interface, and narrative systems.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected `index.html`, `js/world.js`, `js/interiors.js`, `js/lore.js`, `js/util.js`, `js/audio.js`, and `README.md`.
- Confirmed the game loads missing `js/main.js`; reviewed world collision/render APIs, interior portals/evidence records, cast dialogue/alibi data, codex, endings, and UI controls.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, case progression, and existing UI.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining world APIs, NPC data, and interface behavior needed for integration.
2. Implement `js/main.js` using the existing systems and UI conventions.
3. Run checks and browser verification; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: UI structure and module entry point.
- `js/main.js`: Missing game entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town, renderer, colliders, NPC/world support.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments, evidence objects, and portal interactables.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmosphere.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.

## Important Context

How to Investigate

123:
124:

Move

W A S D walk, Shift run, mouse to look. Click the scene to capture the cursor. Esc releases it.

125:

Work the scene

Approach the glinting markers and press E. Every piece of evidence is logged to your casebook. Some clues only resolve in the lab.

126:

Casebook

Tab opens the case file: evidence, suspects, map, the sect, notes. You can fast-travel to known locations from the map.

127:

Interviews

Press E on a person. Ask about the victim, the sect, alibis. Present evidence to break a story. People remember how you treat them.

128:

Warrant

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

129:

Stay human

Sleep, eat, and keep your stress down. The town does not pause for you, and the killer is watching how you work.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.
- Implement the missing `js/main.js` entry point to connect the existing world, interiors, interface, and narrative systems.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected `index.html`, `js/world.js`, `js/interiors.js`, `js/lore.js`, `js/util.js`, `js/audio.js`, and `README.md`; mapped relevant world, interior, narrative, audio, and UI APIs.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, case progression, and existing UI.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining world APIs, NPC data, and interface behavior needed for integration.
2. Implement `js/main.js` using the existing systems and UI conventions.
3. Run checks and browser verification; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: UI structure and module entry point.
- `js/main.js`: Missing game entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town, renderer, colliders, and NPC/world support.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments, evidence objects, and portal interactables.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmosphere.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- `World` exposes `colliders`, `interactables`, `interactablesById`, `interiors`, `scenes`, `keyNpcs`, `genericNpc`, and `genericList`; useful methods include `collides(x, z, r)` and `resize()`.
- Portal interactables have `kind: 'portal'`, `destinationPosition`, and `from`/`to`; evidence interactables have `kind: 'evidence'`, `description`, and `location`.
- `index.html` includes title/help/save-load, HUD, casebook tabs, dialogue, pause, and ending screens.

3: - Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
4: - Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
5: - After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.

7: ## Linux browser and WebGPU capture
8: 
9: - Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
12: - Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
13: - Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
14: - Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
15: - Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
16: - Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
17: - Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.
- Implement the missing `js/main.js` entry point to connect the existing world, interiors, interface, and narrative systems.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected `index.html`, `js/world.js`, `js/interiors.js`, `js/lore.js`, `js/util.js`, `js/audio.js`, and `README.md`; mapped relevant APIs and UI.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, case progression, and existing UI.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining world APIs, NPC data, and interface behavior needed for integration.
2. Implement `js/main.js` using the existing systems and UI conventions.
3. Run checks and browser verification; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: UI structure and module entry point.
- `js/main.js`: Missing game entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town, renderer, colliders, and NPC/world support.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments, evidence objects, and portal interactables.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmosphere.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.

## Important Context
- No files have been edited or committed.
- `World` exposes `colliders`, `interactables`, `interactablesById`, `interiors`, `scenes`, `keyNpcs`, `genericNpc`, and `genericList`; useful methods include `collides(x, z, r)` and `resize()`.
- Portal interactables have `kind: 'portal'`, `destinationPosition`, and `from`/`to`; evidence interactables have `kind: 'evidence'`, `description`, and `location`.

## Objective
- Complete the existing browser-based THE NINTH HOUR as a playable first-person psychological horror detective game set in fictional Mercy Falls.
- Implement the missing `js/main.js` entry point to connect the existing world, interiors, interface, and narrative systems.

## Requirements
- Implement movement and interaction, persistent town/NPC simulation, adaptive killer AI, investigation, procedural cases, and evidence.
- Include fictional sect lore, dynamic events, psychological horror, and multiple endings; preserve narrative ambiguity and avoid an omniscient or invincible antagonist.
- Use historical research only as abstract narrative inspiration; keep crimes and organizations fictional.
- Scale simulation to hardware while preserving persistent state.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking questions; briefly note assumptions on completion.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing browser-based 3D game rather than replacing it with a description or static mockup.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected existing world, interior, lore, utility, audio, interface, and project files; identified APIs and integration points.
- No files have been edited or committed.

### Active
- Implement `js/main.js` to connect movement, interaction, investigation, simulation, case progression, and existing UI.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect remaining world APIs, NPC data, and interface behavior needed for integration.
2. Implement `js/main.js` using existing systems and UI conventions.
3. Run checks and browser verification; report assumptions and checks performed.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: UI structure and module entry point.
- `js/main.js`: Missing game entry point.
- `js/world.js`: Three.js town, renderer, colliders, and NPC/world support.
- `js/interiors.js`: Interior environments, evidence objects, and portal interactables.
- `js/lore.js`: Fictional setting, locations, cast, lore, and endings.
- `js/audio.js`: Procedural audio and atmosphere.
- `js/util.js`: Shared utilities.

## Important Context
- `World` exposes `colliders`, `interactables`, `interactablesById`, `interiors`, `scenes`, `keyNpcs`, `genericNpc`, and `genericList`; useful methods include `collides(x, z, r)` and `resize()`.
- Portal interactables have `kind: 'portal'`, `destinationPosition`, and `from`/`to`; evidence interactables have `kind: 'evidence'`, `description`, and `location`.
- `js/interiors.js` registers evidence and portal interactables; evidence is added across multiple locations including precinct, chapel, library, diner, hospital, bar, motel, and foundry.

Move

W A S D walk, Shift run, mouse to look. Click the scene to capture the cursor. Esc releases it.

Work the scene

Approach the glinting markers and press E. Every piece of evidence is logged to your casebook. Some clues only resolve in the lab.

Casebook

Tab opens the case file: evidence, suspects, map, the sect, notes. You can fast-travel to known locations from the map.

Interviews

Press E on a person. Ask about the victim, the sect, alibis. Present evidence to break a story. People remember how you treat them.

Warrant

Background checks reveal physical traits. Compare them against the lab results, verify alibis, then request a warrant on the Suspects page.

Sleep, eat, and keep your stress down. The town does not pause for you, and the killer is watching how you work.
